introduction: On this second Sunday of Easter, Divine Mercy Sunday, the first Christians devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. In the Gospel, the risen Jesus breathes the Holy Spirit on his disciples for the forgiveness of sins, and Thomas confesses, My Lord and my God. Peter blesses God for our living hope. Let us receive the mercy of the risen Lord.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God in his great mercy has given us new birth to a living hope. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that, like the first Christians, we may be faithful to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the Eucharist and prayer. Let us pray to the Lord.
For priests who hear confessions: that they may be faithful ministers of God's mercy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are suffering trials: that their faith may be strengthened and their hope renewed. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who doubt: that they may meet the risen Lord, as Thomas did. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may be merciful as our heavenly Father is merciful. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: God of mercy, you raised your Son and gave us new birth to a living hope. Keep us faithful to the life of the Church, and make us witnesses of your mercy. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: A living hope
reflection.body:
The Acts of the Apostles gives us a picture of the first Christian community after Pentecost. "They continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer." These four things are still the heart of Christian life: listening to the faith handed down from the apostles, sharing life together, celebrating the Eucharist, and praying. The community shared its goods, "according as anyone had need," and every day "The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved."

In the Gospel, on the evening of the first Easter, Jesus comes to his frightened disciples behind locked doors. "Peace be to you." He shows them his wounds, and he breathes on them: "Receive the Holy Spirit! If you forgive anyone's sins, they have been forgiven them." The risen Lord gives his Church the power to forgive sins. Since Saint John Paul II established it in 2000, this Sunday is also called Divine Mercy Sunday.

Thomas was not there, and he refuses to believe without seeing and touching. A week later, Jesus comes again and invites him to touch his wounds. Thomas answers, "My Lord and my God!" And Jesus speaks to every generation after: "Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed."

Peter's letter is written to such believers: "whom, not having known, you love. In him, though now you don't see him, yet believing, you rejoice greatly with joy that is unspeakable." God has given us "a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead."

This week, look at your own life in the light of the first Christians: teaching, fellowship, the Eucharist, prayer. Which needs strengthening? And receive God's mercy in confession, then show it to others.
